brief_summary:
The goal of this study is to better understand biological characteristics of non-rhabdomyosarcoma soft tissue sarcomas (NRSTS), a rare group of cancers that affect children, adolescents, and young adults. Researchers also aim to identify factors that could help predict how the disease will behave and respond to treatment.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Can advanced molecular analyses improve the classification and diagnosis of NRSTS?
* Can blood- and tumor-based biomarkers help predict outcomes and detect relapse earlier?
* Can researchers identify biological features that may guide future personalized treatments?

Participants aged 0 to 25 years with a recent diagnosis of NRSTS will take part in the prospective study. Researchers will collect archived tumor samples and blood samples during routine follow-up (approximately every 3 to 4 months) and will analyze these samples using advanced laboratory techniques. Clinical information will also be collected over a follow-up period of up to 4 years.

150 participants will be enrolled in the prospective part from 28 investigating centers across France.

Tumor samples already collected as part of your care, together with blood samples taken during follow-up visits, will be stored for future researches.
primary_outcomes: Histopathological profiling of NRSTS tumors
Molecular profiling of NRSTS tumors
title: Prognostic and Predictive Factors in Childhood Soft Tissue Sarcomas

brief_summary: This study aims to evaluate, within a prospective randomized controlled framework, the efficacy and safety of chidamide (an HDAC inhibitor) combined with standard chemotherapy/targeted therapy in patients with initially unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer who have failed first-line treatment. Prior single-cell analysis identified a SULF1-high CAF subpopulation and confirmed its tumor-promoting role, and HDAC inhibitors were shown to downregulate SULF1 expression in CAFs. The primary endpoint is PFS, with secondary endpoints including ORR, DCR, conversion rate, OS, and safety, accompanied by SULF1 expression stratification and translational research.
interventions: Patients receive standard second-line therapy combined with oral chidamide
primary_outcomes: PFS
title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Chidamide in the Treatment of Initial Unresectable Metastatic Colorectal Cancer With High Expression of SULF1

brief_summary: This study aims to investigate the effects and neural mechanisms of individualized temporal interference stimulation (TI) targeting the left nucleus accumbens in older adults with depression. A total of 70 participants aged 60-80 years will be randomly assigned to receive active TI or sham stimulation. Clinical and cognitive assessments, a probabilistic reversal learning (PRL) task, MRI, and TMS-EEG will be used to evaluate changes in depressive symptoms, reward processing, and brain activity. Clinical and cognitive follow-up assessments will be conducted at 1 and 4 weeks after the intervention.
primary_outcomes: Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24)
Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS)
Probabilistic Reversal Learning (PRL) Task
title: Individualized Temporal Interference Stimulation for Reward Processing in Late-Life Depression

brief_summary:
This study is designed for adults who have, or suspected to have, a long-term respiratory (lung) condition such as Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, bronchiectasis, or interstitial lung disease (ILD).

The aim of the study is to help participants become familiar with the clinical trials unit environment and research team before deciding whether they would like to take part in future clinical trials.

Participants will attend a study visit at the clinical trials unit, where they will receive a guided tour of the facilities and undergo a range of routine health assessments. These may include a review of their medical history, measurements of height, weight, blood pressure and oxygen levels, breathing tests, blood tests, heart tracing (ECG), liver assessment, and questionnaires about their symptoms and quality of life. Some participants may also undergo genetic testing if it is clinically appropriate and previous results are not available.

The information collected will help establish a clinical baseline and improve understanding of how respiratory diseases affect people in everyday life. The study will also explore how symptoms and quality of life relate to clinical measurements and other health information.

Participants will be contacted after their visit to discuss any clinically relevant findings and to answer any questions they may have. If a previously unrecognised condition is identified, participants will be advised appropriately and, with their consent, their GP may be informed to support any further care that may be needed.

The findings from this study may help improve the design of future clinical trials and support the development of more patient-centred research.
primary_outcomes: Number of patients indicating willingness to be re-contacted for future clinical trials
Participation feedback questionnaire results using Participant Feedback and Clinical Research Experience Questionnaire
title: Chronic Respiratory Disease Participant Engagement Study

brief_summary:
SMART-BC is a prospective, single-centre clinical investigation evaluating the diagnostic performance of multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) for detecting residual bladder tumour and predicting muscle invasion in patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC).

The study comprises two work packages. WP1 will include 20 healthy volunteers to optimize the bladder MRI protocol using additional clinical sequences without contrast injection, assessing image quality through quantitative and qualitative metrics. WP2 will enrol up to 66 patients with newly diagnosed bladder lesions and suspicious or high-grade urinary cytology, aiming to obtain 33 evaluable patients who undergo pre- and post-transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) MRI and repeat TURBT (re-TURBT), when clinically indicated.

In WP2, mpMRI will be performed before initial TURBT and approximately 3-4 weeks afterwards in patients requiring re-TURBT. Diagnostic performance will be assessed using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value, with histopathology as the reference standard. Standard VI-RADS sequences will be compared with an optimized protocol incorporating additional sequences. Secondary objectives include inter-reader agreement, patient-reported comfort and satisfaction, and preliminary evaluation of healthcare costs and the potential to avoid unnecessary re-TURBT procedures. Safety will be assessed through the systematic collection of adverse events, serious adverse events and device deficiencies.

The investigation uses CE-marked 3T MRI systems and follows routine clinical management pathways. Its long-term aim is to determine whether post-TURBT mpMRI can improve diagnostic assessment and support more personalized management of patients with high-risk NMIBC.
interventions: Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Bladder
primary_outcomes: Diagnostic Performance
title: Diagnostic Performance of Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging After Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour for Prediction of Muscle Invasion and Detection of Residual Tumour in Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer Patients

brief_summary:
This study will evaluate whether a \*\*low-FODMAP diet\*\* can improve symptoms in adults with \*\*functional dyspepsia\*\*, a common digestive condition that can cause fullness after eating, bloating, and upper abdominal pain.

Adults aged 18-70 years with functional dyspepsia diagnosed according to Rome IV criteria will be eligible. Participants must have a normal upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within the previous 6 months, negative testing for Helicobacter pylori, and moderate-to-severe symptoms. People with irritable bowel syndrome, other significant gastrointestinal or systemic diseases, eating disorders, malnutrition, pregnancy or breastfeeding, or recent use of restrictive diets or treatments that may affect the gut will be excluded.

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups will receive standard dietary advice for functional dyspepsia. The low-FODMAP group will also receive dietary counseling from a registered dietitian and follow a low-FODMAP diet for 4 weeks.

Symptoms will be assessed using the PAGI-SYM questionnaire at the start of the study and weekly during the 4-week intervention. Participants will also record their food intake, bowel movements, and any side effects. Dietary adherence will be assessed by comparing FODMAP intake during the study with intake before the intervention.

The study will compare changes in symptoms between the two groups to determine whether the low-FODMAP diet provides additional benefit over standard dietary advice. Safety and any adverse effects related to the dietary intervention will also be monitored.

Written informed consent will be obtained before any study procedures. Participation is voluntary, and participants may withdraw from the study at any time without affecting their medical care.
primary_outcomes: Change in Patient Assessment of Gastrointestinal Disorders-Symptom Severity Index (PAGI-SYM) score
title: Effectiveness of Low FODMAPs Diet Compared With Standard Dietary Advice in Functional Dyspepsia

brief_summary: Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) is commonly performed under moderate sedation with midazolam and fentanyl, but patients may still experience discomfort and procedures can be technically demanding. Dexmedetomidine is a sedative that causes little respiratory depression. This randomized trial evaluated whether adding a continuous dexmedetomidine infusion to standard midazolam-fentanyl sedation reduces patient discomfort and procedural difficulty during EBUS, compared with midazolam-fentanyl alone.

brief_summary:
This randomized controlled clinical trial aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a novel palatal shield technique in reducing postoperative pain and improving wound healing after free gingival graft surgery.

A total of 28 adult participants undergoing palatal tissue harvesting are planned to be enrolled and randomly assigned to two groups.

The experimental group receives a collagen sponge covered by a protective palatal shield made of flowable composite resin, while the control group receives a collagen sponge stabilized with sutures alone.

The primary outcome is postoperative pain, assessed using a 0-10 pain scale. Secondary outcomes include wound size, early wound healing, re-epithelialization, tissue color match, and patient satisfaction.

Postoperative clinical assessments are planned through 30 days after surgery. The study aims to determine whether the palatal shield technique provides better pain control and wound healing compared with conventional collagen sponge dressing.

brief_summary: This clinical trial studies the side effects and how well removing the planning tumor volume (PTV) from radiation therapy (RT) works in treating patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Standard therapy for HNSCC often involves giving RT with chemotherapy; however, this approach is associated with a high level of short- and long-term side effects. RT uses high energy x-rays, particles, or radioactive seeds to kill tumor cells and shrink tumors. RT is planned to be delivered based on three volumes of the tumor. The first is the gross tumor volume which is the area of the tumor that can be seen, felt, or measured on imaging. The second is the clinical tumor volume which includes the gross tumor volume as well as area beyond this to account for disease that cannot be seen on imaging and may have spread. The third is the PTV which includes an area beyond both the gross tumor volume and clinical tumor volume to account for errors that may happen during RT, such as setup error or movement. As the area between the clinical tumor volume and PTV is not cancer and current advances in RT have improved RT accuracy, researchers think that removing PTV from RT may lower side effects while still being an effective treatment. Removing the PTV from RT may safe, tolerable, and/or effective in treating patients with HNSCC.

brief_summary:
The purpose of this study is to assess the effect and effectiveness of Relacorilant on improving the glucose levels in the blood, thus potentially improving glucose control in patients with hard to control diabetes.

This study involves the use of an investigational drug called Relacorilant. "Investigational" means that the drug has not yet been approved by the U.S. Food \& Drug Administration (FDA) for treating "mild hypercortisolism" in patients with diabetes. Cortisol is a "stress hormone". The excess production of cortisol can rise blood sugar (glucose) levels and worsen diabetes. Those disturbances might be corrected by the study medication Relacorilant to improve the state of your diabetes.

This study will evaluate the effects of Relacorilant on glucose control and its safety profile. Although the safety of this drug has been tested in prior human research studies, some side effects may not yet be known.
lead_sponsor: The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio
primary_outcomes: HbA1c (measure of average blood sugar over 3 months) levels
title: Relacorilant in Patients With Poorly Controlled Type 2 Diabetes and Autonomous Cortisol Secretion

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to learn how well and how safely silver diamine fluoride (SDF) stops tooth decay (caries) in baby teeth when it is used in routine dental care. It will include children aged 14 years or younger with caries in their primary (baby) teeth who are treated with SDF at a public primary care dental clinic. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* What proportion of caries lesions treated with SDF do not progress after 12 months?
* How often do side effects occur, such as black staining of the tooth, sensitivity, abscesses, gum or skin irritation, or allergy?
* How satisfied are parents with the treatment? Participants will receive SDF as part of their usual dental care and will attend check-up visits 1, 6, and 12 months after treatment, where the dentist will examine the treated teeth, assess oral hygiene, and ask about diet and any side effects. Parents will answer a short satisfaction questionnaire.
lead_sponsor: Consorci Sanitari de l'Alt Penedès i Garraf
primary_outcomes: Proportion of treated caries lesions without progression
title: Silver Diamine Fluoride for Caries in Primary Teeth in Routine Clinical Practice

brief_summary: This study will test a new virtual reality (VR) Indigenous cultural safety training designed for hospital nurses attending births and caring for sick babies. The training (study Arm #1) includes two one-hour sessions that each include a VR encounter with a virtual Indigenous patient. This will compared to two one hour sessions of unrelated online clinical training (study Arm #2). Participant nurses will be randomly put into one of these two study arms. The study team will then assess whether or not the training improved Indigenous patient care outcomes using live Indigenous actors performing as patients. Participating nurses will be scheduled to assess these mock patients 10-12 weeks after their training. The quality of care they provide during these mock patient encounters will be rated using standard scales. They study hypothesis is that nurses who take the virtual reality Indigenous patient encounter training will have better relational engagement and provide higher quality clinical care during the Indigenous standardized patient encounter compared to nurses who were randomized to the unrelated clinical online training.

brief_summary: This study is designed to explore the efficacy and safety of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) with different delivery routes for patients with functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs). The response to FMT varies greatly, which is related to donor selection, administration route, individual patient characteristics and microbiota compatibility. This single-center, prospective randomized controlled trial plans to enroll 200 FGID patients refractory to conventional medications from OCT 2026 to OCT 2029. Eligible participants will be randomized into a conventional medication group or an FMT group; the FMT group will be further randomized into three subgroups according to transplantation routes: oral capsule, nasojejunal tube and colonoscopic administration. Clinical data, laboratory, imaging and endoscopic results will be collected. Gut microbiota and metabolites will be analyzed before and after treatment. Clinical efficacy and safety will be evaluated at week 12.
primary_outcomes: Clinical response rate at week 12
title: Study on the Efficacy and Safety of Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) in the Treatment of Functional Gastrointestinal Disorders

brief_summary:
Executive functions help people initiate, organize, monitor, and complete everyday activities. Difficulties with these functions are common after acquired brain injury and may also occur in people with long-term pain. A person may understand what needs to be done but still have difficulty starting an activity, maintaining focus on the overall goal, monitoring performance, adjusting a plan, or completing the activity. These difficulties can affect independence, rehabilitation, work, studies, family life, and participation in society.

Goal Management Training is a structured cognitive rehabilitation program designed to help people manage goal-directed activities. Participants learn strategies for stopping ongoing or automatic behavior, identifying the current goal, dividing complex activities into manageable steps, monitoring progress, and redirecting attention when they lose track of the goal.

This multicenter study evaluates the implementation and effects of a Swedish version of Goal Management Training in adults with executive difficulties or reduced working memory following acquired brain injury or in association with long-term pain. The program is delivered as part of clinical rehabilitation at participating centers in Sweden.

The study examines whether Goal Management Training can be implemented in different rehabilitation settings and delivered in different clinical formats, including group-based, individually delivered, in-person, and remotely delivered treatment. The choice of format is based on the participant's clinical rehabilitation needs and the conditions at the participating center. Specific program formats in terms of intensity (five-, seven-, and nine-session versions of Goal Management Training), may be evaluated in separate analyses within the overall study.

Changes are assessed in areas including cognitive functioning, everyday executive difficulties, activity, and participation. The study also examines whether improvements are maintained after the intervention and explores differences in patterns of response between participants and treatment formats.

The overall aim is to improve knowledge about how Goal Management Training can be implemented in Swedish rehabilitation services and adapted to different patient groups, clinical settings, and modes of delivery. The findings may contribute to more accessible and individually adapted cognitive rehabilitation for people with acquired brain injury or long-term pain.
primary_outcomes: Change following Goal Management Training in participant-reported everyday executive difficulties over the follow-up period measured with the Dysexecutive Questionnaire (DEX)
title: Cognitive Rehabilitation of Executive Dysfunction With the Goal Management Training (GMT) - Exploring Variations in Mode of Administration, Frequency and Intensity.

brief_summary:
This is a single-center, parallel-group, double-blind randomized controlled trial conducted at the First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University, enrolling 50 participants with Alzheimer's disease (AD)-derived mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or mild AD aged 50-80 years with ≥4 years of education. Subjects must meet diagnostic criteria per Chinese AD guidelines, show medial temporal lobe atrophy on baseline brain MRI, have a reliable caregiver, and be capable of completing all assessments. Exclusion criteria include severe visual/auditory impairment, non-AD dementia, recent neuromodulation therapy, uncontrolled severe systemic diseases, prominent psychiatric disorders, significant cerebral focal lesions on MRI, and other conditions precluding safe participation.

Eligible participants will be randomly assigned to either the 40 Hz audio-visual stimulation group or the placebo group. The intervention lasts 1 hour once daily for 12 weeks, with a total subject follow-up period of 36 weeks (12-week treatment + 24-week observational follow-up). The primary efficacy outcome is the change from baseline in the 11-item Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive subscale (ADAS-Cog) at the end of treatment. Secondary outcomes include changes in Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and ADCS-Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL) scores across all follow-up visits. Exploratory biomarkers cover plasma Aβ42, Aβ40, Tau-217, gamma wave power on electroencephalography (EEG), and repeat Aβ-PET imaging (if previously performed). Cognitive, functional, emotional, EEG, and blood biomarker assessments will be conducted at scheduled time points. Safety monitoring focuses on intervention-related adverse events such as headache and dizziness, with detailed recording of onset, duration and accompanying symptoms.

Statistical analyses will use two-sided tests at α=0.05. Linear mixed models and repeated-measures ANOVA with ANCOVA adjustment for covariates will analyze the primary endpoint; appropriate parametric or nonparametric tests will be applied for secondary and exploratory outcomes. Baseline group balance will be compared via t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests or chi-square tests. All data processing and statistical modeling will be performed using Python 3.11 and related analytical packages. The trial runs from July 2026 to December 2027.
lead_sponsor: The First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University
primary_outcomes: Change from baseline in the 11-item Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog11) total score at Week 12 (end of intervention)
title: 40 Hz Audio-Visual Stimulation Therapy for AD

brief_summary:
This study evaluates whether robot-assisted bronchoscopy can be used successfully and safely to obtain tissue samples and perform local treatment of lung lesions at Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital, China. Lung lesions are abnormal areas seen on lung scans. Bronchoscopy uses a thin, flexible tube passed through the airways to reach these areas. A biopsy collects tissue to help establish a diagnosis. Ablation is a local treatment intended to destroy targeted abnormal tissue.

The prospective part of the study has three stages: biopsy, an initial evaluation of ablation, and biopsy followed by ablation during the same anesthesia session. Adults enter the appropriate group according to their clinical needs and suitability for the procedure, rather than by random assignment. The need for ablation is determined before the procedure. Imaging is used to confirm the positions of the lesion and instruments, and treatment may be adjusted or stopped if safety conditions are not met.

An exploratory comparison uses existing medical records of patients who underwent biopsy and ablation through the chest wall in separate procedures. Researchers compare this staged approach with biopsy and ablation performed through the airways in one session to explore differences in treatment completion time, time spent in hospital, and procedure duration.

The main outcome for the pathway comparison is the number of days from the first hospital admission to completion of the last planned ablation procedure. Other assessments include whether biopsy provides a diagnosis, whether planned ablation is completed, changes on follow-up scans, and procedure-related complications. After ablation, participants undergo computed tomography (CT) scans at 1 and 6 months, with an additional imaging assessment at either 9 or 12 months.
interventions: Same-Session Robot-Assisted Bronchoscopic Biopsy and Transbronchial Ablation
primary_outcomes: Time from first hospital admission to completion of the last planned ablation
title: Robot-Assisted Bronchoscopy for Lung Lesion Biopsy and Ablation

brief_summary:

brief_summary:
The goal of this observational study is to learn whether external workplace violence (violence by patients, relatives, or companions) is associated with poorer occupational well-being in healthcare workers aged 18 years or older who have regular face-to-face contact with patients or their families. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Do healthcare workers who have experienced external workplace violence in the past 12 months report more negative effects of work (somatization, exhaustion, and alienation) than those who have not?
* How common is external workplace violence, what types occur (physical, verbal, symbolic, digital, or economic), and how intense are they?
* Is external workplace violence associated with working conditions and organizational practices? Researchers will compare healthcare workers who have experienced external workplace violence with those who have not to see if their occupational well-being scores differ.

Participants will complete a single anonymous online survey about their experience of workplace violence, their occupational well-being, their working conditions, and the measures they consider most effective to reduce violence.

primary_outcomes: Collateral effects of work (occupational well-being)
title: Impact of External Workplace Violence on the Occupational Well-being of Healthcare Workers

brief_summary:
This observational study aims to determine how common presbyopia is among working adults aged 30-55 years in Shanghai, China, and identify factors associated with it. Presbyopia is an age-related loss of the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects, which can make reading and other close-up activities difficult.

Participants will undergo eye examinations and complete questionnaires about their vision, work activities, use of digital screens, lifestyle, and need for vision correction. The study aims to obtain valid primary outcome data from at least 1,366 participants. It will also assess how closely the results of the NVC mini-program agree with a professional eye examination. No treatment will be assigned as part of the study.
lead_sponsor: Shanghai Eye Disease Prevention and Treatment Center
primary_outcomes: Prevalence of presbyopia among working adults aged 30 to 55 years in Shanghai
title: Prevalence of Presbyopia (Near Vision Fatigue) and Related Factors Among Working Adults Aged 30 to 55 Years in Shanghai

brief_summary:
This randomized controlled study evaluated whether a daily assisted physical activity program affected blood levels of irisin, adiponectin, and C-peptide in very low birth weight preterm infants. The study also assessed changes in growth and measures related to bone health.

Fifty-four clinically stable infants born at 28-32 weeks of gestation, with birth weights of 1,000-1,500 grams, were enrolled at 1-5 days after birth. Infants were randomly assigned to receive either routine neonatal care alone or routine care plus gentle assisted movements of the arms and legs. brief_summary:
The quadratus lumborum block (QLB) is an established regional anesthesia technique that provides somatic and visceral analgesia for abdominal wall procedures in both adult and pediatric populations. Among its standardized approaches, the posterior QLB (QL2-injectate deposited in the lumbar interfascial triangle at the posterior surface of the quadratus lumborum muscle) and the transmuscular QLB (QL3-injectate deposited in the fascial plane between the anterior surface of the quadratus lumborum and psoas major muscles) are widely utilized.

Although cadaveric and radiological studies suggest that transmuscular QLB yields greater anterior and thoracic paravertebral spread compared to the posterior approach, comparative clinical evidence in pediatric populations remains limited.

The objective of this randomized, prospective, double-blind controlled trial is to compare the analgesic efficacy of ultrasound-guided posterior QLB (QL2) versus transmuscular QLB (QL3) using an identical weight-based dose and concentration of local anesthetic (0.4 mL/kg of bupivacaine 0.25%) in children aged 1 to 7 years undergoing elective unilateral lower abdominal surgery (e.g., inguinal herniotomy, orchiopexy, hydrocelectomy). The primary hypothesis is that one approach will provide superior 24-hour cumulative opioid-sparing analgesia compared to the other.
primary_outcomes: Total Cumulative Opioid Consumption in the First 24 Hours
title: Posterior Versus Transmuscular Quadratus Lumborum Block in Children Undergoing Lower Abdominal Surgery

brief_summary:
This study aims to find out whether using a simple ultrasound measurement of blood flow in the neck artery can help doctors decide how much fluid to give older patients before general anesthesia, and thereby reduce the drop in blood pressure that commonly occurs after anesthesia induction. Older adults are more likely to experience low blood pressure during anesthesia, and such drops have been linked to kidney injury, heart injury, and even death after surgery. Giving too little fluid can worsen organ blood supply, while giving too much can cause fluid overload, lung swelling, and heart strain. Currently, doctors often rely on static measures such as central venous pressure, or on invasive dynamic measures such as pulse pressure variation, but these have limited accuracy or require expensive equipment and invasive procedures. Carotid corrected flow time (FTc), measured non-invasively with ultrasound, reflects left ventricular preload and has shown promise for predicting fluid responsiveness, including in spontaneously breathing patients. However, evidence in older adults undergoing abdominal surgery remains limited to observational studies, and higher-level evidence from randomized trials is needed. We therefore plan a single-center, prospective, randomized, parallel-controlled trial in 70 patients aged 65 years or older scheduled for elective abdominal surgery under general anesthesia. Participants will be randomly assigned 1:1 to an FTc-guided prehydration group or a conventional fluid group. In the intervention group, if FTc falls below 340.7 ms, 250 mL of lactated Ringer's solution will be infused over 15 minutes, and FTc will be re-measured until it reaches at least 340.7 ms, in addition to a background infusion of 6 mL/kg/h started 30 minutes before induction. The control group will receive the same background infusion without FTc-guided adjustment. The primary outcome is the incidence of post-induction hypotension, defined as mean arterial pressure below 65 mmHg or a decrease of more than 20% from baseline within 15 minutes after induction. Secondary outcomes include the area under the curve of mean arterial pressure change from baseline during induction, intraoperative use of vasoactive agents, actual pre-induction fluid volume, postoperative pulmonary complications (pulmonary edema), acute kidney injury, myocardial injury, adverse events in the post-anesthesia care unit, time to first flatus and defecation, and all-cause mortality within 30 days after surgery.

Primary Hypothesis

Compared with conventional fluid management, carotid FTc-guided prehydration before anesthesia induction will reduce the incidence of post-induction hypotension in older patients undergoing elective abdominal surgery under general anesthesia.
primary_outcomes: ncidence of post-induction hypotension
title: In Elderly Patients, Does Goal-directed Fluid Management Using the Carotid Corrected Flow Time (CC-FT) Index, Compared to Routine Fluid Management, Affect the Occurrence of Post-induction Hypotension?

brief_summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and early detection of pancreatic lesions is of great importance for improving patient outcomes. In this study, whole-body imaging with FDG and FAPI will be used to visualize the early development of pancreatic cancer lesions from multiple perspectives, including glucose metabolism, tumor fibrotic stroma, and integrin receptor expression. Furthermore, leveraging the advantages of four-dimensional dynamic long-axial PET imaging, artificial intelligence-assisted lesion detection and analysis will be performed to characterize lesions and differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. The primary outcome was Pain Explanation Competence (PEC) on a previously unseen clinical transfer scenario, assessed without AI access 12 weeks after the intervention by three assessors blinded to group allocation.

brief_summary:
Many wound problems after surgery on the digestive system, including wound infection, are first noticed after the patient has already gone home. Delays in noticing a problem and contacting the hospital can delay treatment. Existing studies come mostly from high-income countries and usually look at only one group of people. No study from Egypt or the Arabic-speaking region was found in the sources reviewed.

This qualitative study will explore what helps and what gets in the way when patients, family caregivers, and nurses recognize, report, and respond to surgical wound problems after discharge from gastrointestinal surgery. Individual semi-structured interviews will be held in Egyptian Arabic, in person or by telephone, at three hospitals in Egypt. The planned participants are 20 patients discharged 2 to 6 weeks earlier, 12 family caregivers, 15 nurses, and up to 4 key informants, for a planned total of 51. Participants will be chosen purposefully to include a wide range of experiences, and recruitment in each group will stop once further interviews bring no new themes.

Interviews will be analysed with reflexive thematic analysis, guided by the Common-Sense Model of Self-Regulation. The main result is a description of the barriers and enablers. Further results are a model of the pathway from noticing a wound change, to reporting it, to the nursing response, and a set of requirements for a nurse-led remote follow-up service.
primary_outcomes: Barriers and Enablers to Recognizing, Reporting, and Responding to Post-Discharge Surgical Wound Complications
title: Recognizing and Reporting Surgical Wound Complications After Discharge From Gastrointestinal Surgery in Egypt

brief_summary:
This is an open-label, multicenter study evaluating the efficacy and safety of marstacimab prophylaxis in approximately 95 male and female adolescents and adults aged 12 to \<75 years with mild to moderate hemophilia A or B without inhibitors who have a severe bleeding phenotype. Eligible participants must have baseline factor VIII or factor IX activity levels \>1% to ≤15% and a history of clinically significant bleeding despite prior treatment with either on-demand factor replacement therapy or routine factor prophylaxis.

The study will compare bleeding outcomes and other efficacy measures during a historical 12-month period of prescribed factor replacement therapy prior to study entry with outcomes observed during a 12-month treatment phase in which participants receive marstacimab 150 mg administered subcutaneously once weekly. Participants will be enrolled into 2 cohorts based on their treatment regimen before study entry: a prior on-demand treatment cohort and a prior routine prophylaxis treatment cohort.

Female participants with severe hemophilia A or B without inhibitors may also be enrolled on a case-by-case basis. Data from these participants will contribute to safety assessments, and separate descriptive analyses of efficacy outcomes will be performed for all female participants.

The study will also evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of marstacimab during a long-term extension (LTE) treatment phase of up to 36 months. Participants who complete the 12-month treatment phase may continue into the LTE phase.

Participants may be in the study for approximately 50 months, including a 12-month treatment phase and a long-term extension phase of up to 36 months.
primary_outcomes: Annualized Bleeding Rate (ABR) of Treated Bleeding Events
title: A Study to Assess the Safety of Marstacimab and How Well it Works in People With Mild to Moderate Hemophilia A or B Without Inhibitors

* Does coconut oil cream reduce the size of oral lichen planus lesions?
* Does it reduce burning or pain in the mouth?
* What medical problems or side effects do participants have during treatment?

brief_summary:
Fear of childbirth and low childbirth self-efficacy are recognized factors associated with negative birth experiences, increased anxiety, reduced maternal satisfaction, and a greater likelihood of obstetric interventions. Although antenatal education programs are widely used to prepare expectant parents for childbirth, considerable variability exists in their content and delivery, and many programs provide limited preparation for the emotional, relational, and organizational challenges encountered during labor and birth.

This randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the effectiveness of the Simulation of Labor (SOL) intervention, a personalized and experiential childbirth preparation program designed for primiparous women involving their birth partners. In addition to standard antenatal education, participants allocated to the intervention group will attend a structured labor simulation that reproduces labor and birth scenarios, hospital care processes, communication with healthcare professionals, non-pharmacological pain management strategies, and potential unexpected obstetric events. The simulation is tailored to participants' individual needs, concerns, and expectations identified before the intervention.

Participants in the control group will receive standard antenatal education alone. The primary objective is to determine whether the SOL intervention reduces fear of childbirth before birth compared with standard antenatal education. Secondary objectives include evaluating childbirth self-efficacy, childbirth attitudes, birth experience, maternal participation in decision-making, obstetric interventions, mode of birth, and selected maternal and neonatal outcomes.

The study will assess whether a personalized labor simulation can improve childbirth preparedness, strengthen parental competence and confidence, and promote a more positive and empowering birth experience.
primary_outcomes: Between-group difference in change in childbirth fear score
title: Simulation of Labor (SOL Study)

Falls are a major health concern among older adults and can affect mobility, independence, and quality of life. Balance training is commonly used to improve postural control and reduce fall risk. However, conventional balance training mainly focuses on physical movement, whereas balance exergames combine physical exercise with cognitive challenges that may help improve both motor control and executive function.

The balance exergame group will participate in game-based balance training using Nintendo Wii Fit, including Ski Slalom, Table Tilt, Tightrope Tension, Balance Bubble, and Penguin Slide. Participants will perform weight-shifting activities on a balance board while responding to visual and auditory challenges during gameplay. The conventional balance training group will perform structured balance exercises involving sitting, standing, and walking activities.

Both groups will participate in supervised training sessions lasting 60 minutes, three times per week, for eight weeks. Participants will undergo assessments before and after the intervention period.

Study outcomes will include fear of falling, cognitive function, executive function, balance and movement performance, and neurophysiological measures of cortical excitability and inhibition assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). brief_summary: Birth weight alone is not precise enough to explain the nutritional status of a newborn baby. The investigators want to understand if there are clues in the body composition of babies born to small compared to babies of the right size that point to why born too small have increased risk of heart and blood vessel problems linked to issues like diabetes and obesity, later in life. Cases (SGA) will be matched with controls (AGA, a baby born not too small and not too large) based on sex, weeks of age at birth (±1 week), number of births the mother has had (same parity). Information about the study will be given in pregnancy. If consent is provided blood samples (mother and cord) will be collected at birth. Additionally, mother's breast milk will be collected. These will be used to measure different molecules in the blood related to health and disease. With the data from this study, the investigators may be able to provide better recommendations during pregnancy that can help optimize baby and infant nutritional status and adult health outcomes.

brief_summary:
A hernia is a bulge through a hole in the muscles of the belly (abdomen) wall. A hernia at the front of the abdomen ('ventral' part) is called a ventral hernia. These happen in a weak area; either on its own or caused by an operation. These can cause pain, get in the way of things people want to do, be upsetting because of how they look, and sometimes can get stuck out (which can cause blockage of the bowels). These can make people's quality of life worse. Because of this, ventral hernias are often repaired in a planned way with an operation.

Expert groups have looked at the evidence from studies, and recommend that the best way to repair all but the smallest ventral hernias is by closing the weakness and reinforcing this and the area around it with an implant. This is called a mesh, and is normally made of plastic. Normally this mesh is placed directly behind the muscles, rather than on top of them. This is called a retromuscular ventral hernia repair.

This used to always be done through the skin over the hernia. This is called an open repair. More recently, it has become possible to do the same operation keyhole, using a surgical robot. This is called a robotic repair. Surgeons think that the end result is the same. But we do not know if how the operation is done affects patients' recovery and experience in the weeks and first few months after surgery.

The aim of this study is to see if people recover differently depending on whether their operation is done open or with a robot. To answer this question, we will run this study in a number of specialist hernia hospitals in the UK. We will ask people who have already decided to have this operation if they would like to take part. We are aiming for 132 people to sign up. They are free to say yes or no, and whatever they say we will not change what operation they have, when or where they have it, and which surgeon does it.

We will collect some information about their hernia and operation when they have surgery.

Then we will contact them in the weeks after their operation, to collect information about their recovery and quality of life. To compare people having robotic and open surgery, in our analysis we will use the information about them and their operation to 'match' them with the person who is most similar in the other group.

We will ask everyone if they want to take part in two extra parts of the study as well. Again, they are free to say yes or no to these as well. The first involves talking to people about their experiences of recovery, so we can understand these better. We can do this in person, on the phone or online depending on what suits them.

The second involves some people coming to our sports science laboratory in Exeter. In this laboratory we will use some simple tests to measure what they can do with their abdomen (such as movement). We see if people can perform these tests, and perhaps see if there is a difference between the operations.

brief_summary:
\# WHAT IS THIS STUDY ABOUT?

This study compares two different treatment approaches for patients with two heart conditions occurring simultaneously: a narrowed heart valve (aortic stenosis) and narrowed or blocked heart arteries (coronary artery disease). Both conditions are serious and, when they occur together, place considerable strain on the heart. The heart must work harder to pump blood through the narrowed valve while simultaneously receiving an inadequate blood supply through the blocked coronary arteries.

\# WHY IS THIS STUDY NEEDED?

Until recently, the main treatment option for patients with both conditions was open-heart surgery. This major operation involves opening the chest, temporarily stopping the heart, replacing the heart valve with an artificial valve, and performing coronary artery bypass grafting to restore blood flow around the blocked arteries. Although effective, combined surgery carries significant risks, particularly in older or frailer patients, including prolonged recovery, longer hospital stays (often 2 to 3 weeks), bleeding, kidney injury, and other complications.

A newer, less invasive treatment approach is now available. This involves replacing the heart valve through a thin tube (catheter) inserted through a blood vessel in the groin, without opening the chest, and treating the blocked coronary arteries using a fine wire, a small balloon, and a metal mesh tube (stent) placed inside the artery. This approach, known as transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) combined with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), typically requires a shorter hospital stay of approximately 2 to 4 days and may allow an earlier return to normal activities.

However, sufficient evidence from well-designed studies is not yet available to establish whether this less invasive approach is as safe and effective as conventional surgery in patients who are not considered at high surgical risk.

This study aims to address this evidence gap.

\# WHO CAN JOIN THIS STUDY?

Adults with severe aortic stenosis and significant coronary artery disease who have been assessed by a specialist heart team as having low or intermediate surgical risk may be eligible to participate.

All participants must be considered suitable for both the catheter-based treatment approach and the surgical approach, based on individual coronary anatomy, clinical characteristics, and medical history.

Patients with previous coronary artery bypass graft surgery, severely impaired left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction below 40%), or a recent myocardial infarction within the previous 6 months are not eligible to participate.

* WHAT WILL HAPPEN IF A PATIENT JOINS THE STUDY?

Participants will receive one of two treatment approaches, selected by a specialist heart team according to individual coronary and valvular anatomy, clinical circumstances, and patient preference:

1. Catheter-based aortic valve replacement combined with coronary artery stenting (TAVI + PCI).
2. Conventional open-heart surgery involving surgical aortic valve replacement and coronary artery bypass grafting (SAVR + CABG).

   Regardless of the treatment received, all participants will undergo follow-up assessments at hospital discharge, 30 days, 6 months, and 1 year after the procedure. Follow-up will include clinical assessments and appropriate cardiac investigations.
   * WHAT IS THE STUDY MEASURING?

   The study will evaluate the incidence of major complications, including all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, serious bleeding, and the need for urgent repeat intervention, during the index hospitalization and within 1 year after the procedure.

   Additional outcomes will include recovery duration, length of hospital stay, and changes in kidney function.
   * WHERE IS THE STUDY TAKING PLACE?

   The study is being conducted at Alexandria University Hospitals and other major cardiac centres across Egypt, with a planned total enrolment of 100 participants.

   \# WHO IS CONDUCTING THE STUDY?

   The study is being conducted by Dr. Moustafa AbdelMohsen Elsayed Madkour, Department of Cardiology and Angiology, Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University, Egypt, under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Mohamed Ahmed Sobhy and Prof. Dr. Tarek Hussien Elzawawy.

KOA is a common joint condition that causes knee pain and makes it hard to keep steady. The study will also look at how this training changes brain activity related to balance.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does balance training help people with KOA stand and walk more steadily?
* Does it ease knee pain and make daily activities easier?
* Does it change brain activity while the brain is at rest?

Researchers will compare two groups:

* The balance training group will do muscle-strengthening exercises plus balance exercises.
* The usual care group will do muscle-strengthening exercises only.

About 74 people will join the study. They will be placed in one of the two groups by chance, with about 37 people in each group. The staff who run the tests and analyze the results will not know which group a participant is in.

Participants will:

* Attend exercise sessions 3 times a week for 8 weeks.
* Do simple balance tasks, such as standing on one leg and walking around obstacles.
* Answer questions about pain, stiffness, and daily activities before and after the 8 weeks.
* Do short walking and balance tests, including the Timed Up and Go test, which measures how fast you can stand up, walk 3 meters, and sit back down. A shorter time means better mobility.
* Stand on a special floor plate that records how much the body sways.
* Have a resting brain scan called functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures brain activity while you lie still.

After the study ends, people in the usual care group who want to will also be offered the same balance training.

brief_summary: This phase II trial tests the effect of early (induction) standard chemoimmunotherapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel and pembrolizumab in preventing more extensive surgery to remove the voice box (laryngectomy), in patients with laryngeal squamous cell cancer that may have spread from where it first started to nearby tissue, lymph nodes, or distant parts of the body (advanced) or hypopharyngeal cancer of any stage. Carboplatin is in a class of medications known as platinum-containing compounds. It works in a way similar to the anticancer drug cisplatin, but may be better tolerated than cisplatin. Carboplatin works by killing, stopping or slowing the growth of tumor cells. Paclitaxel is in a class of medications called antimicrotubule agents. It stops tumor cells from growing and dividing and may kill them. Immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies, such as pembrolizumab, may help the body's immune system attack the tumor, and may interfere with the ability of tumor cells to grow and spread. Response to treatment with chemoimmunotherapy may help guide further treatment, such as radiation therapy with or without cisplatin. Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) is a type of 3-dimensional radiation therapy that uses computer-generated images to show the size and shape of the tumor. Thin beams of radiation of different intensities are aimed at the tumor from many angles. This type of radiation therapy reduces the damage to healthy tissue near the tumor. Intensity-modulated proton therapy is a type of proton beam radiation therapy that uses precise proton beams to target tumors while sparing the surrounding healthy tissue. Cisplatin is in a class of medications known as platinum-containing compounds. It works by killing, stopping or slowing the growth of tumor cells. Giving induction chemoimmunotherapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel and pembrolizumab may be an effective strategy to prevent more invasive treatments, such as a laryngectomy, while improving both survival and quality of life in patients with advanced laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma and hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.

brief_summary:
This study is for adults with advanced or metastatic solid tumours, including colorectal cancer and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. People who have a tumour that has a KRAS G12D gene mutation can take part. This study is open for people for whom other treatment may not have worked or may not be suitable. The purpose of this study is to find out how well a new study medicine called BI 4015092 is tolerated and how it affects these tumours when used alone and together with another medicine called cetuximab. This is the first time BI 4015092 is given to humans.

This study has 4 parts. In all parts, participants receive BI 4015092, either alone or together with cetuximab.

* In Part A1, small groups of participants receive BI 4015092 alone, and the dose is slowly increased to find a suitable dose that people can tolerate.
* In Part A2, participants receive BI 4015092 alone at a selected dose to further check how well people tolerate it and to look for early signs that it can stop tumours from growing or make them shrink.
* In Part B1, participants receive BI 4015092 together with cetuximab, and the dose of BI 4015092 is slowly increased to find a suitable dose for the combination.
* In Part B2, participants receive BI 4015092 together with cetuximab. In this part, participants are put into groups by chance, like drawing names from a hat, and each group gets a different dose of BI 4015092 with cetuximab.

Participants can stay in the study as long as they benefit from the treatment and can tolerate it. During this time, they visit the study site regularly. At these visits, study doctors check participants' health and collect information about any health problems. They also regularly check the size of the tumours and whether the cancer has spread to other parts of the body.

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether a capsaicin-containing diet started before surgery can reduce liver injury and help the liver recover in adults aged 18 to 75 years who are scheduled for surgery to remove part of the liver because of a liver mass. Capsaicin is the substance that makes chili peppers spicy. The study will also assess the safety and tolerability of this diet.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does the capsaicin-containing diet help blood levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), a marker of liver injury, fall more quickly between the first and fifth days after surgery?

Does it improve other measures of liver recovery and reduce liver failure after surgery?

What side effects, including stomach or intestinal discomfort, occur during the study?

Researchers will compare a jelly containing chili powder with a similar-looking placebo jelly containing sweet pepper powder without capsaicin. Both groups will receive the same standard care before, during, and after surgery.

The study plans to enroll 110 participants. Participants will be assigned by chance to one of the two groups, with an equal chance of receiving either study diet. Participants and the researchers assessing their recovery will not know which diet they receive.

Participants will:

Take the assigned jelly three times daily with meals, starting 2 days before surgery and continuing through the evening of the first day after surgery, with a pause for surgery as directed by the study team. The capsaicin group will receive approximately 7.5 mg of capsaicin per day.

Avoid other spicy foods while taking the study diet.

Have blood tests before and after surgery to assess liver injury, liver function, and safety.

Report any discomfort or other health problems to the study team.

Complete follow-up assessments around 30 and 90 days after surgery to check recovery, complications, hospital readmissions, and survival.
primary_outcomes: Postoperative Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) Recovery Rate
title: Effects of a Preoperative Capsaicin-Containing Diet on Postoperative Liver Injury Repair: A Randomized Controlled Trial

brief_summary:
This study is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial in patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D), conducted in two stages.

Stage 1 is the efficacy and safety assessment (TIMES-EFFICACY). A total of 182 T1D patients who meet the inclusion criteria will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to two groups: one receiving mazdutide and the other receiving placebo. The follow-up period is 16 weeks. The primary clinical endpoint is the proportion of patients achieving time in range (TIR) \>70% with time below range (TBR) \<4%. An interim analysis will be performed at Week 8; if the absolute TBR in the mazdutide group increases by more than 5% relative to the placebo group, the subsequent study will be terminated.

Stage 2 is the cardiovascular protective effect assessment (TIMES-CV). During the Stage 1 efficacy and safety assessment, a pre-specified stratification method will ensure that 104 patients with high cardiovascular risk factors are randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the mazdutide group or the placebo group. After completing the 16-week efficacy and safety assessment, these 104 subjects will continue to receive randomized controlled treatment and enter the cardiovascular effect assessment stage, with a total follow-up duration of 52 weeks. The primary clinical endpoint is the change in non-calcified coronary artery plaque volume.
primary_outcomes: Proportion of the participants achieving time in range (TIR)>70 and time below range (TBR)<4% (TIMES-EFFICACY)

brief_summary: Upper Crossed Syndrome (UCS) is a musculoskeletal condition defined by simultaneous forward head posture (craniovertebral angle, CVA \< 52°), rounded shoulders (RSP \> 52°), and thoracic hyperkyphosis (\> 42°). It is highly prevalent in sedentary workers and musicians and is associated with neck pain, shoulder pain, and reduced pulmonary function. This two-arm parallel randomized controlled trial will compare two home-based corrective exercise programs over 12 weeks in adults with confirmed UCS. Both groups (Experimental, EG; Control, CG) perform the same 20-minute program three times per week: diaphragmatic breathing re-education and targeted muscle strengthening and stretching. The EG additionally uses a volumetric incentive spirometer (Coach2, 4000 mL) as respiratory biofeedback and receives active remote reinforcement (biweekly video calls + asynchronous educational material from a physiotherapist); the CG performs the same exercises without the spirometer and receives only minimal adherence monitoring. Outcomes are assessed at baseline (week 0) and at weeks 4, 8, and 12. Primary outcome: craniovertebral angle (CVA) measured by lateral photogrammetry. Secondary outcomes: rounded shoulder angle (RSP), thoracic kyphosis (bubble inclinometer and smartphone inclinometer), pain (Visual Analogue Scale), cervical disability (Neck Disability Index), shoulder pain and disability (SPADI), exercise adherence, and pulmonary function (spirometry: FVC, FEV₁/FVC, MVV) at weeks 0 and 12. Recruitment will take place at the Associació Amics de la Música de Meliana, Fisioterapia A Punto, and Universidad Cardenal Herrera CEU (Valencia, Spain). A total of 96 participants (48 per arm) will be enrolled over a 2-year recruitment window.

brief_summary:
Risk Factors for Outcomes and Postoperative Complications in Patients with Large Intrathoracic Neoplasms (GIANTOR) What is the purpose of this study? The main goal of this study is to evaluate the results of surgery for removing very large tumors inside the chest. While common lung cancers are well-studied, other types of chest tumors (like solitary fibrous tumors or nerve-related tumors) can grow slowly and reach a massive size (over 5 cm) before they are found. Because these cases are rare, there is little data on the best way to operate on them. Researchers want to identify the risks and complications associated with these surgeries to improve patient care.

Why is this study important? Operating on large chest tumors is technically difficult because they often press against or grow into nearby vital organs. Currently, doctors mostly rely on reports of single cases rather than large groups of patients. This study will look at a large multicenter group to provide more reliable information on surgical techniques (such as open surgery vs. minimally invasive) and long-term recovery.

Who can participate in this study? The study includes patients who meet the following criteria:Adults aged 18 years or older.Patients with intrathoracic tumors measuring 5 cm or larger.Tumors that can be either benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous).Patients who underwent surgery with the intent to completely remove the tumor.The study excludes patients with common non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), thymomas, or sarcomas of the chest wall.

How is the study designed? This is a multicenter, retrospective and prospective cohort study. It is led by the IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna and involves six other major thoracic surgery centers in Italy (Rome, Padua, Turin, Pisa, and Milan).Researchers will review medical records of approximately 400 patients who had surgery between January 2005 and December 2024. Data will be collected on:Surgical complications during and after the operation.The type of surgical access used.Patient survival and disease recurrence.

What are the expected outcomes? Researchers hope to:Determine the rate of complications and deaths related to the surgery.Find specific risk factors (like patient health or tumor size) that lead to more complications.Compare different surgical methods to see which works best for large tumors.Measure long-term survival and how long patients stay free of disease after surgery.The results will be shared through scientific journals and international conferences to help surgeons worldwide manage these complex cases more safely.
primary_outcomes: Intraoperative complication rate, postoperative complication rate
Relationship between the development of complications and the presence of pre- or intraoperative risk factors
title: Risk Factors for Postoperative Outcomes and Complications in Patients With Large Intrathoracic Tumors: A Multicenter Analysis

brief_summary: Previous studies have shown that HDAC inhibitors can inhibit SULF1 expression in CAFs. Chidamide, an HDAC inhibitor widely used in clinical practice, has demonstrated good efficacy in advanced breast cancer. Our retrospective study found that the higher the proportion of breast cancer patients with high fibroblast SULF1 expression, the more effective chidamide treatment was. Currently, the third-line treatment for advanced colorectal cancer consists of oral regorafenib or fruquintinib, but their median progression-free survival is only 2.3 and 3.7 months, respectively, and they are associated with significant adverse reactions such as rash, hypertension, and hyperbilirubinemia. The incidence of colorectal cancer continues to increase globally and in Asia; despite advances in advanced treatment, there remains a high unmet medical need, particularly for patients with refractory metastatic colorectal cancer. Chidamide is currently mainly used to treat relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma. Previous clinical studies in China and abroad have found that it also has good efficacy against various malignant tumors, including esophageal cancer, gastric cancer, lung cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, breast cancer, liver cancer, cervical cancer, and leukemia. In summary, the proposed study evaluating the efficacy of chidamide in advanced refractory colorectal cancer with high SULF1 expression has important therapeutic value and high feasibility, supported by solid preliminary data. The objective of this study is to conduct a prospective, single-arm study in subjects with SULF1-high advanced colorectal cancer who have received at least 2 prior lines of standard therapy, to observe the efficacy and safety of chidamide. We hope this study will further clarify whether chidamide, a SULF1 inhibitor, can improve disease response rates, prolong response duration and survival time, and provide patients with advanced disease an opportunity to regain effective treatment.
primary_outcomes: ORR
title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Chidamide in Advanced Refractory Colorectal Cancer With High SULF1 Expression

brief_summary:
Anorexia nervosa is a severe psychiatric disorder associated with substantial morbidity, persistent impairment in psychosocial functioning and quality of life, as well as a high risk of relapse. Although remission is now a major goal of treatment, its definition remains heterogeneous in the literature. The criteria proposed by Bardone-Cone and colleagues are currently the most widely used reference for defining clinical remission in anorexia nervosa. They are mainly based on weight, behavioural, and psychopathological criteria.

However, these criteria do not take into account important dimensions of recovery, such as psychosocial functioning, quality of life, anxiety or depressive symptoms, sexual health, or individuals' subjective perception of their health status.

This study therefore aims to explore the characteristics of patients considered to be in remission according to the criteria proposed by Bardone-Cone et al. and to describe any discrepancies between this remission status and different clinical, functional, and subjective dimensions of recovery.

The investigators hypothesise that patients meeting the remission criteria proposed by Bardone-Cone et al. may nevertheless experience persistent difficulties across different dimensions of recovery, such as quality of life, psychosocial functioning, residual symptoms, anxiety or depressive symptoms, sexual health, or their subjective perception of their progress. Thus, these remission criteria may not necessarily reflect all clinically relevant dimensions of recovery.

This study proposes a multidimensional approach to remission in anorexia nervosa by examining the Bardone-Cone criteria in relation to the different recognised dimensions of recovery: specific residual symptoms, quality of life, psychosocial functioning, functional impairment, anxiety and depressive symptoms, sexual health, and subjective perception of remission.

Unlike studies aiming to propose a new definition of remission, this study seeks to assess the extent to which the criteria currently used can identify patients experiencing satisfactory recovery across these different dimensions. The results may contribute to a better characterisation of the potential limitations of the criteria currently used and inform future research on the assessment of remission in eating disorders.

primary_outcomes: Percentage of participants in clinical remission (Bardone-Cone criteria) with at least one clinically significant impairment on GAD-7, PHQ-9, WSAS, FAST or FSFIl
title: A Study of Remission Criteria in Anorexia Nervosa: A Multidimensional Exploratory Observational Study of Recovery Among Patients in Remission According to the Bardone-Cone Criteria

brief_summary:
What is this study about? When a bone breaks, it usually heals within a few months. In some people, however, the bone does not heal properly (a "non-union"), which can mean ongoing pain, more surgery, and a longer time off work.

This study tests whether a single, local treatment with a medicine called iloprost, given right at the fracture site, can help bones heal better in people who are more likely to have healing problems.

Who can take part? Patients who need surgery to fix a broken bone and who are at higher risk of poor healing. A blood test before surgery measures a certain type of immune cell (CD8+ TEMRA cells). A high level (38% or more) indicates a higher risk. About 533 people will be tested to find 60 participants.

What happens during the study:

Surgery: Everyone receives the standard operation to fix the bone. During surgery, a thin, soft tube (catheter) is placed near the fracture, similar to those routinely used to deliver pain medication to wounds.

Groups: Participants are assigned by chance (like a coin toss) to one of two equal groups:

Group 1: iloprost through the tube for 24 hours Group 2: a harmless salt-water solution (placebo) for 24 hours Timing: In both groups, salt water runs for the first 24 hours after surgery. The next 24 hours bring either iloprost or placebo. Treatment lasts 48 hours in total.

Blinding: Participants, doctors, nurses, and the people who assess the results do not know who receives which treatment. Only the pharmacy staff who prepare the infusions know, and they are not involved in patient care. This keeps the results fair and unbiased.

What happens afterwards?

Participants are followed for about one year (52 weeks), with clinic visits at weeks 6, 18, and 36 and a phone call at week 52.

How will we know if it worked? The main question is whether the bone has healed by week 18, as seen on a CT scan. The study also looks at bone healing at week 36, pain, physical function, quality of life, return to work, and changes in immune cells and blood markers, which help explain how the treatment works.

How is safety monitored? All side effects are recorded and compared between the two groups to see how safe and well tolerated the treatment is.

Why does this matter? Currently, there are few ways to prevent healing problems before they occur. If the treatment works, it could help patients heal faster and avoid further operations. This is an early-stage (phase II) study at a single center. It can show whether the treatment is promising, but it cannot yet prove that it should become standard care.
primary_outcomes: Radiological fracture healing status at Week 18 assessed by CT
title: Local Iloprost Therapy to Promote Bone Healing in High Risk Fractures

brief_summary:
Heart failure is associated with impaired health-related quality of life and reduced exercise capacity. Women remain under-represented in cardiac rehabilitation research, and evidence comparing high-intensity interval training (HIIT) with moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) in women with heart failure is limited.

HIIT-WHEF is a prospective, single-centre, randomised pilot feasibility trial involving 36 women aged 18 years or older with heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction below 50%. Participants will be randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to a 12-week supervised cardiac rehabilitation programme incorporating either HIIT or MICT. Both groups will also undertake individualised resistance training.

The primary objectives are to assess the feasibility and safety of conducting the randomised trial, including recruitment, acceptance, retention, adherence, intervention fidelity, completeness of outcome data and exercise-related adverse events. Health-related quality of life, assessed using the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ), is the key clinical outcome of interest. Peak oxygen uptake, left ventricular ejection fraction and biomarkers will be assessed as exploratory clinical outcomes.

The study is designed to inform the planning of a future adequately powered confirmatory trial. It is not intended to establish definitive evidence of the superiority of HIIT over MICT.

The study will evaluate whether psychological distress is associated with cancer prognosis after adjusting for potential confounding factors, including cancer stage, treatment regimen, and nutritional status.

As an observational study, no experimental treatment will be assigned, and all participants will receive standard anticancer treatment according to routine clinical practice.

Brief Summary

The goal of this clinical trial is to learn which treatment works better for people with alopecia areata, a condition that causes patchy hair loss. The study will compare two commonly used treatments to see which one leads to better hair regrowth and fewer side effects.

Does injecting triamcinolone acetonide into the skin lead to better hair regrowth than microneedling with topical triamcinolone acetonide?

Receive one of the two treatments as part of the study

Attend follow-up visits so researchers can check hair regrowth and monitor for side effects

This can lead to being wrongly diagnosed with dementia. This study will test whether a short, 15-minute guided meditation before taking a memory and thinking test helps older adults do better on the test and feel less stressed. About 60 adults age 50 and older, with lower education and income levels, will take part. brief_summary: Harvesting a free gingival graft (FGG) creates an open wound on the roof of the mouth (palate) that heals by secondary intention. This healing process is frequently associated with postoperative pain, bleeding, functional discomfort during eating, and delayed tissue recovery. Standard care often involves using a custom plastic protective guard (palatal stent) to cover the open wound. Low-level light therapy, known as diode laser photobiomodulation (PBMT), is a non-invasive treatment proposed to stimulate cellular energy production and accelerate soft tissue healing. The purpose of this randomized controlled clinical trial is to evaluate whether diode laser photobiomodulation improves palatal donor site wound healing and reduces postoperative pain and discomfort compared with conventional palatal stent protection. A total of 50 systemically healthy adult participants requiring free gingival graft surgery will be randomly assigned to receive either diode laser photobiomodulation or a customized palatal stent. Wound healing will be monitored over a 28-day follow-up period using 3D digital intraoral scanning to measure wound size reduction, hydrogen peroxide testing to confirm complete skin re-coverage (re-epithelialization), clinical healing indices, and visual color match with surrounding tissues. Patient-reported outcomes, including pain levels, daily painkiller tablet consumption, difficulty chewing, burning sensations, bleeding episodes, and overall satisfaction, will also be recorded
primary_outcomes: Percentage of Palatal Wound Closure

The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does adding ketamine to the standard SGB anesthetic (bupivacaine) improve treatment effectiveness compared with bupivacaine alone?

Does SGB reduce PTSD symptom severity compared with no injection (control group)?

Researchers will compare participants receiving SGB with bupivacaine, SGB with bupivacaine plus ketamine, and no injection (control) to determine whether SGB reduces PTSD symptoms and whether ketamine enhances the effects of the procedure.

Participants will:

Be randomly assigned to receive SGB with bupivacaine, SGB with bupivacaine plus ketamine, or no injection during the randomized controlled trial portion of the study.

Complete questionnaires and clinical interviews assessing PTSD symptoms, anxiety, depression, functioning, and quality of life.

Participate in follow-up interviews to discuss their experiences with the treatment.

Invite a family member or support person to complete a questionnaire about observed changes in symptoms and functioning.

Have the option to receive a standard SGB procedure during the study extension phase, if eligible.

This study will enroll approximately 126 participants and aims to improve understanding of how SGB works for PTSD and whether ketamine can enhance its therapeutic effects.
lead_sponsor: The Royal's Institute of Mental Health Research
primary_outcomes: Change of the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) total symptom severity score
Change of the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) total symptom severity score
